utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Djeric, before we continue your examination, I have to deal with a few small matters. So if you would be patient enough to wait for a second. First of all, there is a revised translation of P65 tab 157 which is also P64A, tab 730. The registrar is instructed to insert the corrected version into the record in place of the old incorrect version, to the extent the parties have not yet received copy of that revised translation, they are available with the registrar. It concerns the minutes of the 5th session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held during an imminent threat of war on the 10th of June 1992. Then I was informed that the Defence has selected two portions of the video in relation to the bridge and has prepared an English transcript of it. May I take it that the Prosecution is informed about which portions they are?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course. I copied the video -- I beg your pardon, the e-mail to my learned friends. Mr. Harmon has already replied very efficiently, if I might say, and with a corrected translation of the second portion which I will look at briefly during the course of the afternoon but I'm sure I will accept. I'll not sure what his position is so far as the transcript of the exchange on the bridge is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had intended to have that looked at but the phones were down and I was unable to connect with my language assistant. I propose that we defer this matter briefly. I will discuss this matter with my language assistant who will review the translation against the actual video and then I will have a response to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That goes to the details of the transcript and, well, the language of the transcript. Do you expect to raise any fundamental objections against --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore it now has become more or less a matter of technicality rather than any matter of dispute between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful to know, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I was informed that the Defence has been provided with an English version of the Islamic Declaration, and is looking into whether and if so what portions of that document it wishes to tender as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour we are three-quarters of the way through that process. It requires some input by me. I will do that during the course much this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sent one further e-mail to one of the Legal Officers. Simply asking for clarification as to the -- Your Honour's comments as far as objections to exhibits is concerned. Your Honour yesterday used the word "filed," that the objections be filed. What we wanted to know was whether Your Honour really meant filed. Quite happy to do that if that is what the Chamber requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we asked for written submissions on it and that communication could be through an e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour used the word filed, for what it's worth, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most important for us, Mr. Josse, is that if we take decisions on objections against admission into evidence, it should be formally registered somewhere, if we have not dealt with it in court orally and therefore where it does not appear on the transcript of this -- of the hearings, then of course we should find a way of registering it in such a way that it becomes part of the records of this trial, which does not necessarily mean that not prior to formal filing, in an informal way, the Chamber and the Prosecution could be informed about the substance of any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be some objections. I will make sure that they are in written form by this time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then when filing actually takes place, I mean, if we are informed about the substance and if the filing later on would take place later on, but of course, would then be exactly in the same wordings as what we worked on earlier, then I don't think that it would be a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I emphasise realistically the Defence's last opportunity to file for the next three weeks is by tomorrow, 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore I say that if it's in written form there and if later we have an opportunity to verify what is then finally filed, of course you could file in such a way that you say, hereby we file formally what has been brought in written form already to the attention of the parties and then make the filing in that way, it's mainly our concern that everything finally is on the record, if ever another Chamber, for example the Appeals Chamber, would have to look at it, that it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They don't have to dig through all of our e-mail exchanges in order to find out what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Djeric, thank you for your patience. We will now continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, may I ask you, in the beginning of May 1992, were you informed by Miroslav Deronjic about an attack on a village called Glogova and a continuing operation to transfer the Muslim population out of the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I say that with full responsibility, and I don't know that man either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because this Chamber received evidence that when someone, I think it was Mr. Deronjic himself, came to see you, that you very much disagreed with what had happened, and to just summarising, that Deronjic went to see Djeric who became very angry when he heard about the attack on Glogova and the forced transfer of Muslims. Djeric asked who had ordered the attack and Deronjic replied that he himself had done so. Does this in any way refresh your memory on this matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pure lie, a pure lie. I assure you with full responsibility. I don't know that man at all and he never came to see me. Do you understand that? As for that -- well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that your recollection does not enable you to confirm what was said in relation to a visit to you in which the matter has been -- that's a more broader --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no visit. It's a pure lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's for the Chamber finally to find out if there is contradicting evidence what evidence would be to be believed, if any at all. But I observe that you strongly oppose such a description of events at the time. Then let me -- because you'll not be able to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I was angry when people came there. I didn't know anything about it. People were there, like, for two days in Pale. I was the only one there. I don't think that there was anybody else from the leadership who was there, and then I happened to hear through my driver that these people were there. I got very angry. Who was doing this? Who is doing this? And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who is doing what? I mean, were you informed about such an event even if Mr. Deronjic didn't visit you or --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody informed me. I didn't know anything about this. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The testimony of course says that -- or at least the evidence tells us that you were not informed about it but that you were told after it had happened.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When people arrived there, when they had been there for two days already, I heard from my driver that somebody brought these people there from Bratunac. Do you understand that? Then I did my best to resolve the problem of those people there. I assert that nobody talked to me before that about any attack on Glogova, the transfer of people. I don't know anything about that. I mean, somebody told this Deronjic -- I mean on the basis of what can he claim that I was angry? I mean, there was someone who was conveying what my reaction was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be some confusion about the following. My question was focusing on the attack on Glogova and in more general terms on an operation to transfer the Muslim people -- population out of Bratunac municipality, where it seems, if I understood you well, that you are referring to something that might be related, I'm not saying it's not, but about people from Bratunac arriving in Pale, which is not necessarily people from Glogova, but --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So did I understand you well that you were -- that you got acquainted with the presence of a larger number of people, as you said, who stayed for two days in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about the consequences or rather I learned that they were from Bratunac but I didn't know what they were doing there, who brought them there, nothing, as for the attack on Glogova and so on and so forth, as for Deronjic coming to see me, that is a pure lie. It's a pure lie. I state that with full responsibility. I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's, then, for a moment forget about a visit of Deronjic and about an attack on Glogova. What did you learn about a number of people from Bratunac municipality, so therefore not necessarily related to Glogova, arriving in Pale, staying there? From whom did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then did you ever see those people in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them? You are talking about, that they stayed two days. Do you know what happened after these two days?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, well, I heard that there were people there, that they were exposed to some unpleasant things and so on, and I took measures immediately to have that problem resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply to see what could be done with these people, what kind of solution could be offered to them, a solution for them, allegedly they expressed a wish, that's what I was told, they expressed a wish to go to Sarajevo and I did everything for them to be transferred to Sarajevo some way, because obviously -- well, for them to go back would be pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you learned that they were exposed to some unpleasant things. Could you specify or could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know much about this. Allegedly, they were forcing them there to sing some kind of songs or something like that. Well, certain provocations, and, well, I mean, I didn't like that. I didn't like that. In a way, I was at my wits' end in a way. I thought that this was inhumane, that this problem with these people had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you seek to resolve the matter just on your own or did you discuss it with anyone else? Did you discuss it within any meetings or sessions with others?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No sessions. I mean, I simply sought solutions on my own, transportation vehicles, well, to have this problem resolved. I was surprised that no one had informed me through some official channels that these people were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you gain any impression on whether it was or had become general knowledge that these people had arrived in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I mean, well, possibly, but I did not know. Now, whether the general environment was aware of this, I don't know. I cannot tell you about that. But I certainly -- well, I mean, well, I must have been among the last to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said you acted on this information. You told us that you learned this from your driver. Would you usually take action just on the basis of information of your driver or did you verify in any way whether what your driver had told you was correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, as soon as he told me, I expressed an interest in this, to find out what was going on. You know, I didn't know anything about this. So once it was, well, confirmed that people were indeed there, I took measures to have the problem resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who confirmed to you that people were indeed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I mean, I don't remember. I communicated through these people who were around me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you name them or give us the qualifications of the people around you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, they were people from the police before. Andjic is the name of one of them, then there is another one called Kovacevic, Drazinko Kovacevic. I don't know who else was there. They helped me resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you addressed these people, were they -- did they give you the impression that they were not aware yet and that they had first to verify or did you, from their reaction, gain the impression that they were already aware of the presence of those people from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got the impression that they knew about this. Well, I mean, that that was certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you receive any information about the number of people from Bratunac that had arrived in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Well, perhaps a couple of hundred. I don't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do I understand you well that you say this was the approximate, it was more or less the scale or the size of this event, a couple of hundred? I mean, could it have been ten or could it have been 2.000 or what makes you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say a couple of hundred, I don't know the exact number, you see, do you understand what I'm saying? I'm speaking tentatively that it had to do with the large number of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We received evidence that General Subotic testified that General Subotic offered his resignation to the Bosnian Serb Assembly in August 1992, since he disagreed with the way General Mladic conducted military affairs. The problem, as we were told, was that General Mladic acted as commander of the Main Staff and that General Subotic warned the assembly that he could not work under two commanders at the same time, that is under Mladic and Mr. Karadzic. Was the government and the Minister of Defence in the military chain of command at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government and the Defence Minister, the government was not, definitely. As for the Defence Minister, I don't think that he was either. The government was connected to the military through the budget, through the -- some civilian issues and so on. As far as I understand it. But I have to tell you that any way, this connection, this link, between Karadzic and Mladic and Subotic and particularly between Subotic and Mladic, wasn't, how shall I put it, there was always some dispute there, and I'm not quite clear what it was all about. Simply, the army did not accept General Subotic, actually at the time he was a colonel. Later he became a general. He didn't have the command. He couldn't have -- he couldn't have had any command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Subotic consult you before offering his resignation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. He had no reason to consult me on these matters, because I was out of that very early. The decisions of the National Security Council were given to Karadzic. They were in Karadzic's hands. So we had nothing to do with that. The general did complain about communications with the army because he did have difficulties in performing his duties as Defence Minister, but in that sense, I really couldn't help him much because I didn't have any powers in relation to the army, to the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move to another subject. It is alleged, Mr. Djeric, that you were present at a Bosnia and Herzegovina government meeting on the 3rd of April 1992, at which the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership was in attendance. This meeting allegedly was convened due to the outbreak of violence in several municipalities, including Bijeljina and Banja Luka. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Maybe you can just remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I reminded you about the date. At least I gave you the date, I gave you those who were present.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know on what basis I could have attended those meetings as minister without portfolio in charge of development. I really don't remember. Perhaps this was convened by the Presidency or something, because of that. So this is why I'm asking you just to remind me a little bit because these problem was something that mainly the Presidency members dealt with, Biljana Plavsic and so on and so forth, at the time. The army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the evidence we received says that Presidency members were there, specifically Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic, as well as you, Mr. Djeric, and General Kukanjac, and to give some more information about what we learned about this, as I said, it was -- the meeting was convened because of the outbreak of violence in several municipalities, including Bijeljina and Banja Luka, and we received evidence that it was of particular concern in this meeting that in Bijeljina, Arkan's men might have killed civilians. That was what we learned from this evidence, a concern that was discussed during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably -- well, I wasn't there by myself in that group but it's possible that we were all called to convene, all the ministers. This is possible, because this was discussed. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that you know that it was discussed but your recollection doesn't tell you that you were present during this discussion.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say -- I mean it's possible that I was present, but I don't believe that I was just part -- or amongst those members or those names that you mentioned. It's possible that I was there but that there was a wider circle, a larger number of people there, and it's possible that General Kukanjac was there, I mean I think it was a brief meeting. We didn't spend too long discussing matters, but what I'm saying is that there were more of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So from your answers I take it that you then were present, if you can tell us how long the meeting took, and if you are able to tell us that the circle of persons present was wider than the persons I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again, I do recall a meeting but I don't know whether that was because of Bijeljina or because of the events in Sarajevo. I cannot remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have seen some minutes of the kind shown to you yesterday, which you said they were not authentic, some minutes of Presidency meetings which were attended by military personnel. Could you tell us how often the military leadership and the civilian leadership would meet in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the military leadership contacted Karadzic. Karadzic was the one in command who commended people, decorated people and so on and so forth. The civilian leadership did not have any intensive contacts. The rest of us. Maybe from time to time, if they happened to be there, then they would be invited, because in the style that Karadzic chaired the meetings, anyone could attend the meeting, anybody who happened to be there, he would bring them in, he convened the meetings and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that occasionally took place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally, yes. In the first half of this period, practically, when I was serving. It was very seldom that this happened. But then, as the government began to stabilise itself more and more, then these visits or arrivals were more frequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We also received evidence -- and I quote from that evidence -- that on the 25th of May, so it's a little bit later in time, that you tasked Mr. Stanisic to, and I now literally quote from that evidence, "Gather information and deliver a report to the government on the security of people and property" in the Bosnian Serb republic. For the parties I'm quoting from P763 at paragraph 237.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I wonder -- while I'm on my feet, I wonder if Your Honour also has the reference for the piece of evidence cited just now in relation to the 3rd of April meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 3rd of April, let me just -- I think it's a tape recording of the 64th session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 3rd of April, and that's P980.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This evidence I just quoted from, that you tasked Mr. Stanisic to gather information and deliver a report to the government on the security of people and property, this evidence tells us that you received a report in June 1992 from the MUP, stating that an exhaustive account could not be prepared because the Bosnian Serb republic was in a high state of flux, that personnel were overcommitted and communication with various regions was not always regular. First of all, do you remember to have tasked Mr. Stanisic with gathering information and deliver a report on the security of people and property?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Does that refer to the government or the National Security Council, that acted in that way? Because I must ask for your understanding, for your indulgence, because the term "government" was often confused, mixed up. Karadzic frequently used the term "government" when he was appearing, when some statements were issued for the international community. It would be as if it were -- was from the government, he would use the term "government"; simply that term was misused a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then do you remember that you tasked Mr. Stanisic or that someone else tasked Mr. Stanisic with gathering information and deliver a report to either the government or any high governmental organ, including the Presidency, a report on the security of people and property?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically then but I would charge my people from the government to inform the government, to make a report, so that this could be then reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember if you charged your people to make a report on the subject I just mentioned? Do you remember what kind of information you received?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but what I'm saying is that I had problems constantly with the relevant ministry because I kept asking for certain information all the time but I wasn't receiving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember how many times you asked reports from Mr. Stanisic on matters such as the security of people and property?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that I was in office, I kept requesting that from the time in June when the government was formed, from June to October. I asked information on several occasions from that department, information on various issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you ever receive a written report on it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I did; sometimes it took a while; sometimes they would be detailed; sometimes they would be quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us approximately what kind of information was in those reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. I cannot remember. It was a long time ago. There were lots of strictly confidential, all these abbreviations were used, so I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by there were lots of strictly confidentials? Would that mean that you should not share information with these reports with others or what do I have to exactly understand by lots of strictly confidential?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the Ministry of Internal Affairs would usually, you know, they thought everything was confidential, more or less, so even if they did make the reports, these reports would be very short. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then correctly understand, if you say that you received reports but that reference was made to the confidentiality of certain information which would then not appear in those reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I did receive them, but then I no longer received them. You know, sometimes I received them and if I did, they were brief, they were short reports because they were used to that particular style of work. That's why I'm saying they were short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these reports discussed in government sessions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if it was a written report, it would be discussed just like the report of any other ministry. Every ministry made reports, and this also applied to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, when the report did come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did these reports you received, or the substance of these reports, were they also brought to the knowledge of members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no need -- the government had no need to inform because the government was linked to the Presidency. The government only dealt with that section of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that had to do with law and order, budget, financials, but not the use of the police. The use of the police was something that the president was in charge of, so the minister directly communicated with the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you -- were you ever able to conclude, on the basis of the discussions within the Presidency or perhaps I should say the five, as you called them yesterday, that the others present during those meetings of the five were acquainted with the existence of such reports and the substance of such reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they could have been informed about it via Karadzic, in that part that relates to the use of police for military purposes and so on. As for these other questions that had to do with regular, daily affairs, salaries, equipment for the police, daily assignments, that kind of thing, that was not interesting. This was something that was conducted in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started your answer by saying, "I assume that they could have been informed about it via Karadzic." So your assumption is about a possibility, and a possible way of -- a possible channel through which they would have been informed. My question was whether you were ever able to conclude on the basis of the discussions you attended that they were informed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This problem was constantly discussed, the problem of the communication, of the ministry and the minister with the government, and they were informed in that context. I kept complaining in a way that this was a problem for me, that the minister was responsible to someone else, that I did not receive the necessary information, complete information, that you couldn't work like this, and if the minister belonged to the president, then I wanted this to be known. So they were informed or aware of this in that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever, when you complained about this, receive an answer saying, "We in the Presidency, we do not receive information either"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get an answer. Karadzic always stood up for him, defended him. I had a problem. This is what I said yesterday. The government was marginalised. The government simply did not have the proper information and was not able to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move to another subject. This is alleged, Mr. Djeric, that you were present at a meeting held on the 2nd of September 1992, with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Mladic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Subotic, General Gvero and others. Do you remember any meeting on the 2nd of September in which the persons mentioned were present, among others?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember that particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to see -- one of the issues -- one of the issues to which reference was made was strategic goals, and according to the evidence, these strategic goals would roughly correspond to what were called the strategic objectives. Perhaps first of all, are you aware of what was called strategic objectives at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, as for the strategic goals, everybody formulated strategic goals and everybody spoke about strategic goals in their own way, so everything there is quite muddled, how a particular person understood that particular thing. I understood that it was simply protecting the political interests of the Serbian people within Bosnia and Herzegovina, since those interests were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. Are you aware that, in the Official Gazette, once, a document was published which contained six strategic goals? So I'm not talking about what Mr. A or Mr. B or Mr. C or Mr. D said, but about what was published in the Official Gazette. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, because there were different channels through which materials were sent to the official gazette for publication. That is to say from different organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the source of the information that appeared. You as a Prime Minister, did you not gain knowledge of what was published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't know what strategic goals. Remind me, please. I mean, I had communication with the gazette in terms of the government sending its decisions through the Secretariat to the gazette. That is to say -- please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik and I had the same thought because -- well, probably because the facts are these: Mr. Djeric was not the Prime Minister at the time of the publication of the Official Gazette. Does Your Honour remember there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might have made a mistake there. If so, I haven't got in mind the exact date of the publication. But if that is true, I should have left out of my question, as a Prime Minister, but I think the answer of the witness is -- well, let me just say: Did you ever learn from the Official Gazette, whether it was prior to or while you were Prime Minister or at any later date a publication formulating six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember that. Do you understand what I'm saying? Things were very dynamic. There were these incredible dynamics. I did not manage to follow everything and to see what was being published where and what was being written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to say that from the Official gazette, no, I did not read that and I was not kept abreast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that a lot of people expressed themselves on strategic goals or strategic objectives. Was there any common denominator in what those people or would the one say the strategic goal is to gain access to the mountains and the others would say, no, it is about building bridges or -- could you tell us whether, when people were expressing what strategic goals were, whether you could try to give a common denominator of what those persons comprised in these strategic objectives or strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, what was understood by that was the protection of the interests or the promotion of the interests of the Serb people within the state interest of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wish to remind you that the referendum, which was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina, had seen the Serb people outvoted or rather their democratic right to self-determination was done away with. I mean, these strategic objectives were something that people quite simply, well, saw as a quest for seeking appropriate solutions for this imbalance, rather, this lack of balance. That is to say resolving the political status of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its constitutional position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I, for example, would mention access to the sea, would that ring a bell, in terms of whether you ever heard strategic goals to be formulated, including this by far more concrete aspect, far more concrete than the rather general aspects you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that too. That was discussed as well. But I did not talk about that, because that was not -- I mean, within my area of interest. I never said a word about that. You can -- you cannot find anything about me having talked about that. I never talked about that. But things like that could be heard, yes, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said this was discussed. Where?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I heard that -- and people wrote about it. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. Sort of in different newspapers. Well, there was this sort of discussion. I mean, unofficially and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would mention a few others -- would you please let me -- for example, establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities, does that ring a bell as part of or a formulation that ever came to you of any strategic goals or objectives?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in that sense, it seems to me that at one particular assembly, at the very outset, I mean, something like that was being said, but I did not say anything about that. Some borders were talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you come back again and again as to what you said. I didn't ask you that. I was just asking you about your awareness of strategic objectives being formulated, not necessarily by yourself. Another one: Set up a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. Does that sound familiar to you in the context of the formulation of strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was discussed too. And quite often at that. This was being used politically. I remember that. But my understanding of all of these things was, well, quite simply, that this was something for political use, where representatives of the party, especially those who were conducting policy, I assume at the behest of the people, they were going around and talking about some kind of borders. But as far as I can remember, all of this was focused on Bosnia-Herzegovina, within Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say in the sense of some sort of reorganisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would be in accordance with the will of all three peoples. It was my understanding that this was a certain continuity of the pre-war talks on regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll not go with you through some of the others. Could you remind me exactly when were you appointed Prime Minister? Was that -- I think you said yesterday it was -- when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked about that, sometime mid-March, possibly it was the 24th of March. I mean, yesterday I -- well, that's the date that I remembered. It was the date of an assembly meeting held in Pale. Possibly then. Then I, well, then I was appointed Prime Minister-designate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I started these series of questions with a meeting on the 2nd of September 1992, with Mr. Karadzic, Mladic, Krajisnik, Subotic, Mr. Gvero and others. I said that strategic goals were referred to during that meeting. We now went through strategic goals that were formulated and that were discussed. Does this refresh your memory as far as the 2nd of September 1992 meeting is concerned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, no. I don't even know where it was held. I mean, quite simply, I cannot locate this in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you. Mr. Stewart I'm a bit puzzled by the publication in a time when Mr. Djeric was not Prime Minister. According to my information the adoption of and the publication of the strategic objectives was the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The publication in the official gazette was -- that was an assembly session on the 12th of May in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. They were adopted according to the publication on the 26th of November 1992. The 12th of May, yes, I made a mistake; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. While I'm on my feet I'll just say with the witness present, Your Honour, the exhibit P980 that Your Honour referred to, as the evidence reference in relation to meeting of the 3rd of April. We are inquiring whether there is any further evidence reference beyond simply the exhibit itself. I'll put it in those very bare terms right at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I remember, that is the -- let me just look at my notes. I think we have some transcript pages. I have not verified them at this moment but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This very moment doesn't matter. Might I inquire, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's somewhere 18188, 18189 but to be quite honest I haven't got this available immediately for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll track down those pages, Your Honour, may I but if Your Honour has any more specific information that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I have any I'll check during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, yesterday you said [In English] I was bothered somewhat by Krajisnik's indiscriminate and uncritical relationship to Karadzic. I think they were friends but I still think that his attitude should have been different." [Interpretation] Sir, could you please develop on this? Why did you assess the situation as such?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I proceeded from the fact that Krajisnik was president of the parliament, that he had some strength, and that he was a manage who belonged to the party and to its highest organ. Quite simply, I mean he had to have a stronger influence over Karadzic. I mean for things to be resolved. I mean, to have the government affirmed, to have a state based on the rule of law affirmed. Do you understand what I'm saying? All the time this remained sort of within the bounds of a party state and within the bounds of the party. So it's from that point of view. I mean, it is my assessment or my impression that he could have been a bit more critical. I mean, more active towards him. That's what I meant. In view of his party position, in view of his position as speaker of parliament and, in particular, as his friend from earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in your answer, you seem to say that some of the actions conducted by Mr. Karadzic could have been countered by Mr. Krajisnik. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't mean in that sense only but, well, that can be talked about too, but primarily in the sense of making Karadzic see reason. I mean, how should I put this? A person should bring him to a situation where he should think a bit differently, not as a psychiatrist or as the leader of a party or a political leader and so on and so forth, but that he should think on the basis of some facts and by way of having the legal state of affairs function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, could you please talk in pragmatic terms, in practical terms? Just give me one example of a situation, of a decision that was made, made by Mr. Karadzic where Mr. Krajisnik could have given him another advice, could have influenced him to change his mind? What exactly are you thinking about? So please, I beg you, be practical.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, as far as the position of the government is concerned. One can say, we have to have a government, we have to affirm the government, the government has to, I mean, well, keep things under control, break down these feudal masters down there and so on and so forth. I mean, to have the rule of law applied. So he could have influenced him from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let's talk about those feudal masters. And let's be realistic. Talk in a -- tell me exactly who you're thinking about when you're talking about those feudal masters.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the heads or rather chiefs of various Crisis Staffs of various entities of various municipalities individually, and so on and so forth. We had a situation in which what was evident was the primacy of the local level, down there, in relation to what was up there on the top, you see. I mean, they had this party line primarily, and they set store by that, and quite simply, they would side line the government and they would go directly to the Presidency. I told you about that yesterday. They went directly to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, let's talk about something else. You told us that neither Mr. Stanisic nor Mr. Mladic bore much attention to government meetings. They didn't really care about government meetings. Sorry, it was Mandic and Stanisic [interpreter's correction].

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't herd heard your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The translation didn't come through, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] I thought I understood that neither Mr. Stanisic nor Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation into English? There is no interpretation into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, interpretation can be heard now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have no problem but Mr. Djeric had a problem in --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps Judge Hanoteau would, you be so kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One of the microphones is off. It doesn't matter. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I understood that you were telling us that neither Mr. Stanisic nor Mr. Mandic paid much attention to government meetings. I thought I understood that most of the time they weren't even there. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday and I confirm that. I mean, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: Were there any occasions where you were actually able to blame them for this, to directly tell them, "You're not behaving like ministers should behave"? Did you ever discuss that with either one or the other or both?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, individually and together, more or less the entire government had a position on that, that the two of them were those who were not working for the purposes of the government. More or less they were with Karadzic all the time. I asked for them to be replaced and that could not come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did they answer you when you blamed them for this? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either Mr. Mandic or Mr. Stanisic. They explained themselves, they gave you an explanation for their behaviour, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They behaved as if I couldn't touch them, that they had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you to tell me what they answered to you, what was their answer when you blamed them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, they just waved their hand and go away. There was this misunderstanding all the time and so on and so forth. Once, Karadzic -- once, Stanisic said that he would cool me off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, I'd like to ask you some questions about the Ministry of information, the Minister of Information, sorry. What exactly, what role did he play exactly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a party man, a party man. For the most part, he kept hanging around the party. I mean, he was in the party. And he only recognised, well, the top echelons of the party. He was in the main board there, I guess, and here in the government he held the position of Minister of Information. Well, quite simply, he was a party man, to put it briefly, an activist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he in charge of circulating party politics? Did he use the media to that end?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, he, well, somehow I find this inseparable. I mean he's a party man, there was a party state. There was no opposition there. One can assume that, well, that he did not leave aside party interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer my question. As Minister of Information, did he -- did he -- did he use the media? Did he use the media to just circulate the party line, his own party line?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I cannot tell you about that competently because I'm not a member of the party. I cannot go into that. I cannot say. I'm just telling you that he was on television all the time, on the radio, I mean with journalists, all the time, sort of, well, probably he was promoting himself first and foremost and then everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Do you remember that at one point in time the federal MUP sent an emissary to take over the paramilitaries and to control them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Davidovic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal -- you mean from Yugoslavia? Yes. I -- it does ring a bell. That's up there in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What exactly does this remind you of? Who asked for him to come over to the territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not. This could only be done by the minister for internal affairs or someone but I did not. I did meet him in Bijeljina, though, that's where I got to know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it rings a bell about Bijeljina but what does it remind you of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was some unit which was up there to secure some kind of order. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no further questions for you, Mr. Djeric, at this time. We'll have a break. I already asked the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I yesterday invited the parties to give it some thought as to how much time they thought they would need for further questions to Mr. Djeric. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Stewart and I did have a brief opportunity to discuss that at the time, both of us indicated to each other we thought that the time, full time made available by the Chamber would not be necessary. I wish I could estimate with more precision but I certainly expect for example to conclude my questions by the end of the day and hopefully considerably earlier but that's about the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the end of the day, that would mean -- let me just see, it's now ten minutes to 4.00, up to 7.00 is a little bit over three hours. We need two breaks, one of 25 and one of 20 minutes. That would be a little bit over two hours. Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's very difficult for me to say anything specific. I'm not going to need all day tomorrow or anything like that, Your Honour but what would be particularly helpful, Your Honour, would be if it were possible to have a slightly longer break because we would really like to go and see Mr. Krajisnik to see where we are on this. Your Honour knows that that's often something we do and it's often valuable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, would you still be able to finish today if we would grant a little bit extra time for the breaks? Well, let's say to have a break of a little bit over half an hour now and perhaps if need be the next break to be 20, 25 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you're flattering with a degree of precision that I'm afraid I can't claim. But I don't particularly see the problem, in light of the fact that I do think that given my discussions with Mr. Stewart that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What might be a helpful suggestion, Your Honour f Mr. Tieger was going to go pretty near the end of the day we could have the discussion with Mr. Krajisnik at the prison tomorrow morning which would actually be more valuable in a way to us. If it looks as if Mr. Tieger is going pretty near to the end then we could do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to do the following, Mr. Stewart. If we have a break now of well, let's say half an hour until 25 minutes past 4.00, try to use your time and see what you can do in this break, and if need be, there might be another opportunity at a later moment to complete your consultations with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I just had in mind that Mr. Tieger was on time for today. That was part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but what his answer he'll be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed perhaps it would be a totally justified response to my trespassing time limits several times at 7.00 -- that today we really have to stop at 7.00. We adjourn until 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you'll now be examined by Mr. Tieger, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Court asked you a few questions concerning, among other things in that period of its questioning, an order of 26 April 1992, concerning Crisis Staffs. And that could be found at page 55, 54 and 55, of yesterday's transcript. You looked at the document of that date, which listed actions to be taken concerning the Crisis Staffs, and you said you never came across this document, at page 55, and that it was a pure forgery. I'd like -- now the Court exhibit that was shown to you at that time was found at tab 6 of the Court's documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assure that Mr. Djeric has tab 6 in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document entitled excerpt from the instructions for the operation of Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that as far as I can recall I didn't say it like that. I just said that I didn't recall this document because if we are talking about April, you know, this -- we are talking about April --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric I'm not asking to you explain --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Government --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Go ahead, you can finish that, and then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the transcript of yesterday's session will speak for itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we read immediately to -- Mr. Djeric I read from the transcript of yesterday, where you started saying that in this point in time there was no government, there was just a Prime Minister-designate, then secondly you said who signed there? Who signed this document? I don't find this clear, I mean this document, I mean, this is a forgery too. And a few lines later, you explained, you said well, I asked you what made you conclude that it was a forgery and you said, because, well, quite simply because it refers to me and I see that I never came across this document, especially because certain prerogatives are given here and I never dealt with this, you see, so it is a pure forgery, a set of instructions was sent to Crisis Staffs signed by Karadzic and me but meaning that they should be careful as to how they behaved. So two times you said it's a forgery and I think I'm referring to the -- this document, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So two times you said it, not once, twice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't think that it's this document that we are talking about but maybe some other documents that we looked at. As for this document, I said that I do not recall because at that point in time, the government did not exist. It could have -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to read what is on the transcript of yesterday's hearing. You also said that you do not recall that you came across this document but you twice said that it was a forgery, and if you think that there is an error in translation, please tell us, we'll check it on the basis of the original words spoken by you and see whether it's properly translated. I just wanted to put this to you and leave it to Mr. Tieger to ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at this point, Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, let's proceed, please. At this point I'd like you to look at two documents. They are two copies of the excerpt from the instructions to the operation of Crisis Staffs. And Mr. Djeric I'll tell you that these two documents, and I'm more than happy if requested by the Court or the Defence to provide affidavits in connection with this, that these documents were obtained directly from the Republika Srpska government archives. And I'd like you, in particular, Mr. Djeric, to look to the stamp and signatures that appear on that document and confirm, if you will, please, that those are your signatures.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature. This is not my signature. I simply see that this does have -- is under the heading of the government but the government didn't exist at the time. I was appointed Prime Minister on the 24th of April and if I understood the date correctly yesterday, the date here is the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We are going to look at the date you were appointed Prime Minister, Mr. Djeric, but isn't it the case, in fact, that you were nominated and accepted the position of Prime Minister at the 12th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on March 24th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I distinctly got the impression here that you were trying to suggest that you had only been appointed so recently that this document couldn't have anything to do with you. In fact, you had been appointed a month earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of April, and this is the 26th of April. I'm talking about the government. The government was not formed most probably before the end of May because this is a government document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're not suggesting, are you, that this document was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the archivist for Republika Srpska because it was found some place other than the Republika Srpska government archives, are you? In other words you're not disputing that these documents were recovered from the RS government archives, are you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing it. It's just that I don't remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who do you say signed this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature is not mine. I mean, I simply -- I do not recall sending this myself. I think that yesterday I said that there was an instruction that President Karadzic drafted but that was already the National Security Council, and that's where I put my signature, there. That's what I do remember. But as to the government and me doing that alone, I don't recall that. So we really need to see exactly what we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This Court has received evidence, Mr. Djeric, that this document was received and acted upon in various municipalities, for example, I'll just give a couple of examples, Hanson tab 100, we find the 1 May 1992 decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality, which repeats almost verbatim the instructions contained in this document. Similarly, we see from the book of minutes at tab 79 of the Hanson documents, from the Kljuc municipality, that one of the members of the Crisis Staff acquainted the other Crisis Staff members with the Crisis Staff operating instructions. And I won't go on except to mention that a witness who appeared for the Defence, Mr. Pasic, confirmed that in Bosanski Novi, these instructions were received and acted upon, indeed he said at page 19729, "I have already mentioned in my testimony that the Crisis Staff had no choice and could not have undertaken anything else." Are you disputing, Mr. Djeric, that the Bosnian Serb authorities, and let's just leave your involvement in this aside for the moment, issued instructions to the Crisis Staffs for their operation in late April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that. If you understand me correctly, I'm talking about an instruction that was signed by President Karadzic and I signed it -- I could signed it, and the idea was to draw attention of the Crisis Staffs or rather the local authorities to the obligation for lawful conduct. We had no other way or other solution other than to draw their attention to their conduct, to their work, in respect of adhering to laws, laws of Republika Srpska, international regulations and so on. This was supposed to serve as a caution or a warning, a document that was meant to deter all those factors from illegal conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, excuse me a second?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether that is that document or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's just what I was going to ask you. We've heard a great deal and I'm sure we'll hear some more about your commitment to the rule of law and preventive actions. I understand that's what you're trying to tell us again. Is this document, before you now, the same document that you say was issued by you and Dr. Karadzic in connection with the Crisis Staffs or is this a different document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really state something like that. I really don't remember. I know that the document that I'm talking about indicated the need for respecting laws, regulations for creating living conditions and so on. In that sense, respect of law, caring for the population, the people, a humane approach to everyone. That's what I remember. But again, I repeat, this is a document that was signed by President Karadzic and me, and at that point as the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, those two documents will need numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document, Your Honours with ERN number 01246834 and 835 would be given P1286. And the other document with the ERN number 01245649 and 50 would be P1287.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you were also asked by the Court to look at the minutes of the government session held on 24 May 1992. That occurred at pages 61 through 62 of yesterday's transcript. And once again, you said, at page 62, this is a forgery too. That's tab 7. Now, Mr. Djeric, this is a document that was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor in two different ways. First, directly from the government archives themselves.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 7, the minutes of the government session of May 24. Mr. Djeric, I started to indicate to you, this is a document that was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor in two different ways: First, directly from the government archives of Republika Srpska; and second, in response to an official request for assistance to Republika Srpska for, among other things, the government, the minutes of government sessions in May, and this document was sent by the Republika Srpska authorities. Is it your contention, sir, that the archives of Republika Srpska are maintaining forged minutes of the government and that the government of Republika Srpska has been sending forged minutes of certain sessions to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm not asserting that. But about this -- these minutes, this question under A3, that it was a greed that the president of the assembly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please read more slowly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidents of the Presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik is organising meetings, I'm saying that it's not possible that the government entrusted Mr. Krajisnik to organise these meetings, so what I'm saying is that these minutes are in a way questionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What is so astonishing to you about the possibility that there was a discussion with Mr. Krajisnik or a member of his office resulting in some understanding that that action would be undertaken which was subsequently relayed to the government at this session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, it is implied that Mr. Krajisnik was present at the meeting and that it was agreed, as it is stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Djeric, to another allegedly forged document. At pages 41 through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before doing so, Mr. Djeric, you -- one second, please. One second, please. Yes. You now say, "so what I'm saying is that these minutes are in a way questionable." Yesterday, you said, "These minutes simply are a forgery." There is quite some difference between the two lines. I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that all of the evidence you gave yesterday, unless there is a translation error, and even translation errors can be simply verified, that the Chamber finds it very important that if you draw conclusions that it should be clear that these are conclusions. You said yesterday, not only these minutes simply are a forgery, you said they are not authentic. I would just draw your attention to, now for the second time, you're taking back more or less what you testified after having given a solemn declaration yesterday. Mr. Tieger you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to look next, Mr. Djeric, at another document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, can I just -- I mean, I was just speaking freely. It was my interpretation. And now I see that you're now approaching it in a legal manner and I apologise. If you understand me, I was just saying, well, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We want you to tell us exactly the truth and use your expressions in such a way that you fully can guarantee that what you say is right. Mr. Tieger now has put to you two occasions that where you said yesterday it was a forgery, that you take at least quite a bit of it back at this moment. And it's a reminder for the testimony still, don't speak -- well, of course, speak freely; but speak precisely as well. With your education and background, we could expect you that even if you're not a lawyer that you can make a distinction between doubt you have in a document and to say it's a forgery, it's not authentic. I just wanted to remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] JUDGE ORIE: Mr. Djeric, Mr. Djeric, please listen to the next question and give an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At pages 41 through 44 of the transcript yesterday you were asked about and discussed the document found at tab 3, the minutes of the session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska of 9 October 1992 and once again, Mr. Djeric, you said those are a forgery. Now, were you just speaking freely and indicating that there were some aspects of the document about which you had some question or do you still maintain those were a forgery for the reasons you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just please help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab -- tab 3.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about this document because I do not recall Mr. Krajisnik ever chairing over a meeting or session. I was explicit there. Not only from that aspect but also from the aspect of the type of topic that we have here. For example, Slavonski Brod is mentioned. I don't remember that at all as being talked about. Further, I am seeing here Krajisnik, Koljevic, Branko Djeric. Koljevic died and there is only the two of us now. So I simply am saying what I said already about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. That there are aspects of it that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember -- all right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the basis of your recollection, you conclude it's a forgery and want the court to rely on that. Now, Mr. Djeric, one of indeed the point that you emphasised most strongly to the Court yesterday in arriving at your conclusion that this document was a forgery was the one you mentioned twice, you mentioned it, the first, at the beginning, page 41, and then again at page 44, which was that these are a forgery because 9 October is the day you resigned in Prijedor at the assembly session and of course this document doesn't say that this Presidency session took place in Prijedor. You remember saying that, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes -- said that but the meeting in Prijedor, as far as I can remember, was when I resigned, and this has that date, the 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The meeting in Prijedor, Mr. Djeric, took place on the 30th, 31st of October, not on the 9th. Isn't that right? That's a matter of record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can remember is that it was the 9th. I have no reason about the dates. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Couple of other aspects --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean this can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. It can be checked and we'll check it in a moment, in fact. Let's look at a couple of other things you said. You also said at page 42, I believe, looking at the reference in the document to the Boban-Izetbegovic agreement that you didn't remember that. Don't recall negotiations between Boban and Izetbegovic, right? That's another basis for asserting to the Court that this document is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I had nothing to do with the agreement. I did not take part in that. I mine. I had nothing no do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was such an agreement. You just didn't take part in it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Except that you wanted to assert the non-existence of that agreement as the basis for your conclusion that this was a forgery or your assertion that this was a forgery?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, I mean, I don't know about that. I don't know about that. I mean, I did not participate in that. And this was not discussed at the Presidency. I mean, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a couple of documents, that's extra 31 and 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those will need numbers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They would be P1288 and P1289, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The first document, which I believe is 1288 all throw I couldn't see which one was marked which way?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I gave the numbers before we got the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but now we have to find out which one is which. Shall we say that the 6th of October document has the number P1288, that is -- seems to be a letter with attachment from Mr. Trbojevic to a certain Radovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1288, Mr. Djeric, a document dated 6 October, 1992, sent by Milan Trbojevic, the Deputy Prime Minister, your deputy, to Dr. Karadzic, Radovan, "sending the draft agreement we proposed," and as you can see, looking at the agreement on the subsequent page, it's an agreement between Republika Srpska, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and more specifically involving Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban. And as we can see for Republika Srpska, your name appears as well. "Republika Srpska represented by Dr. Branko Djeric." How is it, Mr. Djeric, that an agreement in which you participated, which is reflected in the minutes of another session, approximately the same time, indicate in any way that that document is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please, I won't saying that it was a forgery. I just said that I did not know of that agreement. Boban-Izetbegovic. I don't know about that. Have a look at this here. You see that it has to do with some document that does not bear my signature. Further on, there is a reference here to a cease-fire. It is true that there were talks between the representatives of Herceg-Bosna and Republika Srpska, so that is correct. I took part in that delegation but I was not the head of that delegation. The head of that delegation was Nikola Koljevic, who was not mentioned here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how is that relevant, Mr. Djeric? Mr. Djeric, the simple fact is this: You were shown a document, you said it was a forgery, you were asked why, you said in part because it refers to this agreement, meaning that such a reference must be so untrue as to indicate that the document is a forgery. And now we come to find out that you participated in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please, I mean, I think we don't understand each other. I said in relation to the Boban-Izetbegovic agreement, Boban-Izetbegovic, I mean this is the Croat and the Muslim side, Boban and Izetbegovic, whereas this has to do with the agreement between Republika Srpska and, I mean, the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Take a look at the next document, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Take a look at the next document, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
