utterances.text: You see, you see, that it's being done through the Deputy Prime Minister and not me. I was not even head of the delegation there. I mean, you know, if you ask me, well, I'm sorry, but if you ask me whether I know anything about the agreement between Republika Srpska and Herceg-Bosna I would have said yes to you. But Izetbegovic and Boban, no, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was a great mystery, that agreement between or proposal for an agreement between Izetbegovic and Boban, huh? Was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were participating in the discussions between Republika Srpska and Herceg-Bosna. Take a look at 1289. The next document. That is the October 10th, 1992 article entitled Muslim Croat cooperation in brief. Which begins, Zagreb, 8th October the president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban agreed to form a joint command of the Croat and Muslim units in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Split on Tuesday, 6 October. That was a fairly newsworthy event at the time, wasn't it, Mr. Djeric, to many people, and particularly to the leadership of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you I don't know anything about that. I don't know anything about that. I was on the periphery, as far as these developments were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for the details of that, Mr. Djeric, I'm simply exploring your assertion before this Court on repeated occasions that documents were forgeries. That reference to you pointed to and relied upon in the October 9th Presidency minutes to assert that it was a forgery is no basis at all, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I did not remember. Those were my grounds. That's the basis. I did not remember any discussion of an agreement between Boban and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nor do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, Mr. Tieger is putting to you that, if you do not remember something, and if an event, the same event you do not remember, is reflected in a document, that you should not easily conclude that you are -- that it must be a forgery because you don't remember what is contained in that document. That's what Mr. Tieger is putting to you. I don't think that he's exploring further details about this agreement at the moment; Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's quickly take a look at a couple of other aspects of --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you may listen to the next question of Mr. Tieger and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the Presidency minutes of 9 object in front of you at this point, Mr. Djeric, also indicate that regarding the military -- that's on page -- only a two-page document, page 2 of the English, under the second conclusion, the second paragraph, regarding the military operation in Sarajevo the following was concluded, to halt artillery bombardment and achieve this through the main command of the Serbian army because UNPROFOR is exerting control, 2, a way should be found to implement this conclusion the possibility of demilitarising the town of Sarajevo has been considered from the military and every other aspect, the good and bad sides of this attempt, et cetera. As well, look at the reason why this should not spread to the entire territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in that connection, I'd like you to look at the government minutes of October 12th a few days later. That's extra 23. It seems to need a number, Your Honour although it may be that it simply didn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the same time if we could distribute also the next one is number 24, minutes of government session and we'll have those available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Minutes of the 55th government session Your Honours will be P1290.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the 56 will need a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The minutes of the 55th government session are already in evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour we are getting rather confused by numbers. We've got extra numbers we got the exhibit numbers which we can handle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most important is that we all have the same document in front of us and Mr. Tieger is now going to explain to us what number it has already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The 55th session is P64A, P65, tab 70, P583, tab 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm -- I do not find any P64A tab number, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 670, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 670.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The one that's confusing us is the reference to extra 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- is merely my indication to our case manager and I apologise for that. I will -- I can appreciate that you are taking it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Djeric, looking at the minutes of the 55th session I have just asked to you look at that portion of the Presidency minutes of 9 October referring to the possibility of demilitarising the town of Sarajevo and, in that connection, we see, in the minutes of the 55th government session, that the government was briefed on the asked terms regarding the demilitarisation of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide as far as the page is concerned, Mr. -- I think we found something on page 3 under RAI [phoen] 1. No, no. I'm sorry, I have to rely upon you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what about page 7, the second item from the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour that is exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you wanted to draw the attention of the witness to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, if you look toward the latter part of the document you'll see a reference to Biljana Plavsic and UNPROFOR talks, also PTT services. That should help orient you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, if you would look at the last three digits 567, at the top of the page, where the page starts with item 40, a few lines further down, it seems that it starts with the word Vlada, and at the end of that line you'll find the word demilitarisation and Sarajevo. Have you found that? It's the semi-last page. Semi-last page in B/C/S. Yes. It starts with RAI 40, questions and proposals, and then please look at the second item there. You found it? Could the page be put on the ELMO so that we can see -- yes, you found it? Could the document be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you read the text to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The government was briefed on the asked terms regarding the demilitarisation of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the right document in front of you? Mr. Usher could you please put it on the ELMO so that we can is have a look at it. Mr. Djeric could you follow it on the screen? No, we have to be further down. It is the semi-last page but it seems -- no. Could I have a look at that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Appears to me, Your Honour, as the Court is pointing out, the second paragraph under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the 56th session. It's the 55th session we have to look at. Mr. Usher please the 55th session. Semi-last page, B/C/S. Top of the page, top of the page, please, Mr. Usher. Yes. Mr. Djeric, you found it, second item under number 40, after the introduction. Have you found it? Could you please -- could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that it's clear on the screen of Mr. Djeric. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, that's the government minutes under that agenda item reflect a discussion about the same issue that is the possible demilitarisation of Sarajevo that was discussed at the Presidency session of October 9th, 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could look quickly at the 56th session, agenda item 12?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher could you assist Mr. Djeric? Now we are at the document I just returned to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is P64A, tab 661.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you'll find that at page 7, and at the ERN 01245575, you'll see those numbers at the top of the page and you'll see agenda item 12 at the top of the page. If you still have the minutes of the Presidency session of 9 October, the one we've been looking at for sometime now, you'll see that the minutes reflect the following, at the Presidency session of October 9th the status of the Serbian university is being considered the need to elect a rector, financial assistance, et cetera. In that connection I ask you to look at item 12 of the 21 October government minutes, the 56th session which state, "the decision appointing Vojislav Maksimovic as the Sarajevo university rector was adopted." Again, Mr. Djeric, does the minutes of the government session held on 21 October reflect a discussion and indeed a decision about the same issue addressed at the Presidency session of October 9th; that is, the need to elect a rector. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I remember that. I mean, this was discussed and the rector was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that factor would tend, I take it, given your reliance on your memory in connection with the allegations of forgery to support the conclusion that the minutes you looked at before are indeed authentic, that is they reflect a discussion that was taking place roughly contemporaneously with another government body or another body of the Serb -- of the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I'm talking about this, I mean I'm talking about the appointment of the rector. I remember that. I do not remember the other questions. As a matter of fact, I'm not even sure whether this has to do with a proposal for the position of rector. I mean, I do not remember which organ was making a decision, was it the assembly or the government. I remember it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, the issue is that Mr. Tieger puts to you that some of the items that were discussed in -- on at least according to the minutes you said were forgeries, that some of the items discussed according to these minutes appear soon afterwards in government meetings in a similar way as they had been discussed in the -- at least as we see them discussed in the minutes of the 9th of October and what Mr. Tieger puts to you is whether you would agree that this would be contrary to a conclusion that these minutes of the 9th of October are a forgery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- well, as for the record of the 9th of October, I said -- well, I said what I said, that Krajisnik, as far as I can remember, never chaired a Presidency session. That is one thing. And then I remember -- I mentioned all these other things. For me, those minutes are unreal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated earlier that we would look at a document in connection with your assertion that this document is a forgery, because you resigned in Prijedor on that date, and, in fact, we do not have as the Court and the parties know, the transcript of that session. But we had an opportunity to look at the minutes of that 21st session of the assembly of Republika Srpska and I'd ask that that be provided to you at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger it has been established that both the 55th and the 56th session are already in evidence so the numbers 1290 and 1291 are vacant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll provide the Court with the exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply observe this that when numbers are used earlier on and then they are vacated it doesn't make the subsequent reading of the transcript any easier although we end up with documents, this happened a million times in this case anyway. We end up with documents in evidence more than once but it actually helps the reading of the transcript later if we leave the numbers as they are because they have been used in the course of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless it's immediately established in the same transcript, but we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just observed that practical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour this is P583, tab 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, as you can see, these are the minutes of the 21st session of the assembly of Republika Srpska held on 30 and 31 October and the 1st of November, and those minutes reflect, at page 9 of the English and page 7 of your version, in B/C/S, Mr. Djeric, that the Prime Minister gave his resignation to his position orally but that the assembly did not decide about the proposal on the vote of confidence in the resignation of the Prime Minister and as we have seen in other evidence, that issue was raised again at the 22nd assembly session held in Zvornik, at the end of November 1992. Mr. Djeric, this clearly indicates, correct, that your resignation or the submission of your resignation in Prijedor didn't take place on October 9th but took place at the end of the month or beginning of the next month?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, these dates, maybe I don't remember them very well. I kept thinking it was the 9th of October. I'm not challenging this. These are things that can easily be checked out but then at this session in Prijedor I not only resigned orally, I resigned in writing, because a resignation was required in writing. I tendered it in writing, I signed it, and that was that. The assembly, well, as far as I'm concerned, I had resigned. And the assembly at its next session in Zvornik adopted that resignation. They could have adopted it at the 21st session in Prijedor too. They could have. Now, why they didn't, that's a different matter. And why this entire -- well, process was dragged on for two months, I mean that is probably something that was required due to political needs but I resigned orally and in writing. It was signed at this session Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We discussed the April 26th instructions at the outset of this session. And when you were asked about that yesterday, the Court asked you immediately before addressing the 26th April instructions about an excerpt from the assembly session of 24 March 1992, that is the 12th session. That was at page 54 of yesterday's transcript. And there, the Court was asking you about and quoting from the assembly in connection with the tasking of the government regarding an operative plan for assuming power. And you professed to have no recollection of that session, I think you said specifically what assembly, where was this assembly held, as far as you could remember there was no assembly and then the questioning moved on to the 26th April instructions. Now, Mr. Djeric, this particular session, from which the Court quoted an excerpt concerning the government's tasking to prepare an operative plan for assuming power, was, in fact, the date on which you were nominated for and accepted the position of Prime Minister. And in that connection, I'd like you to be presented with the transcript of the 12th session and I'd like you to look at page 43 of the B/C/S, that's contained at pages 24 through 26 of the English. You see that, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You'll want to turn to page 43, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would appreciate if you read it literally to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we see the chairperson indicating, "I hereby open up for discussion the proposal for the premier designate for our government who shall propose members for our government at the next session on Friday. At the next 13th session which will follow today's 12th session, ministers in certain fields will be proposed," and then it goes on, no one wants to take the floor, already no other nominations, the assembly unanimously adopts the proposal that Dr. Branko Djeric be elected the premier designate of the future government of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the chairman notes this would Mr. Djeric like to say something and indeed, Mr. Djeric, as you can see, you do, beginning, Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, deputies, one should say something at a moment like this. You remember that session now, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as Mr. Krajisnik indicated in the remarks immediately preceding yours, there would be two sessions, and in fact there was a subsequent session on the 13th which was held approximately 25 minutes after the 12th session adjourned. So you were the last speaker, Mr. Krajisnik indicated that we conclude the 12th session, and then there was a short break, beginning at 1555 hours and the 13th session then began at 1620 hours on the same date. And if we look at, Mr. Djeric, the 13th session, page 13 of the English and I'll provide you with the B/C/S and if you will look at page 10?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found that, Mr. Djeric, page 10 of the document, which will be -- oh, you have not even received the document. Mr. Usher could you please give page 10 to the witness. THE USHER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, where are we finding the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 13 -- not the page but the actual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood that the parties and the Court were informed to bring certain sessions, including this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, we weren't -- the 17th session, the parties which is only us, actually, if you take a way the Prosecution, we were told the 17th session, which we brought with us. That's the only information that I'm aware of so the Court has the advantage over us here. 14

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it seems to have been an oversight and my apologies I'll read it slowly if it helps. I think it's material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay, I was just puzzled. We will proceed like that. I accept the apology. Of course these things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On page 13 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S, Mr. Djeric, we first see Mr. Krajisnik speaking. So a conclusion is instructed by which the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be given the assignment to draw up a plan of assuming power and rendering operational the authorities in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government will propose the plan to the assembly on Friday, if we arrange for an assembly to meet on Friday. And you, Mr. Djeric, speak immediately after, saying and confirming, "The government will have the duty to draw up an operational plan and to submit it for adoption. We shall do our best to speed things up, to gain time wherever possible. There is no reason to think that we are running late in assuming the power because a lot has been accomplished by now. Please do not take things in your own hands. You will receive your instructions and you will proceed as instructed." It is correct, Mr. Djeric, that the government, in fact, was tasked with creating an operational plan for assuming power as confirmed explicitly and directly by you at that session, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in -- there was no conclusion adopted in this sense. Perhaps an operational plan was discussed, the implementation of the assembly decisions because here it also says you will receive instructions and you will -- I mean who? Who am I addressing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djeric, I have considerable number of ideas about that but you're the witness and you said it. Why don't you tell the Court please who you were addressing and what the operational plan was instead of suggesting that you didn't even know this session took place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't know. Yesterday I said that it was at Pale. I did not dispute in any way that session, that meeting. But here we are talking about the takeover of power and addressing, you know, as if that -- there was somebody that I was addressing. These were just deputies of the Serbian people in their own assembly. They were not the ones who were being assigned any roles. The government operational programme could have been discussed in accordance with assembly conclusions. So that could have been a topic of discussion. But as for instructions or issuing instructions to anyone, I think that that simply -- something is not quite clear here. The government did everything within the assembly, within the sense of the assembly decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, what you said and what you were referring to is not quite clear to you and you don't recall what the operational plan was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what the operational plan was or if there was any talk about takeover of power there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What do you mean if there was any talk about taking over power? You said there was no reason to think that we are running late in assuming the power. Mr. Krajisnik said the government would be given the task to draw up a plan of assuming power. Of course, there is talk about assuming power. It's right there in front of you. Now, do you remember the operational plan for that purpose or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. We are talking here about drafting an operational plan and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government didn't exist at the time. What government, when there was no government then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, if there was no government, what was there then at that period in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prime Minister-designate was named at that session. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there a kind of interregnum, that the council of ministers was still functioning or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't remember. It preceded the government. But I mean, as to whether it had a practical role, practical force, whether it worked or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wasn't it true that the appointment of ministers in the new government was discussed during this session after a decision had been taken to relieve from duty the council of ministers of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do remember that at this meeting, after -- well, two ministers were proposed, the minister for internal affairs and minister for foreign affairs, and that was all at these sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they proposed or were they elected, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were proposed or nominated, and the assembly accepted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the proposal was put to the assembly and that it was, for example, talking about Mr. Buha, that it says the assembly unanimously adopted the proposal to elect Professor Aleksa Buha -- isn't that -- accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes. I think I said that. It's true that Buha was nominated and Mico Stanisic was nominated also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when I asked you were they proposed and were they elected, Mr. Djeric, the answer was just yes to these two, because your first answer was that they were proposed and you said, you added to that, they were proposed, and you mentioned the two ministers, and that was all at these sessions where it appears that these two ministers were not only proposed but that this proposal was adopted by the assembly. So it was not all at these sessions that they were proposed but the two of them were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were proposed, and the assembly confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nomination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger I'm looking at the clock but also listening to Judge Hanoteau who wanted to ask one question but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, in the minutes of this assembly session, on page 5 in the English version, I read the following: "[In English] Professor Branko Djeric speaking, I have completed my consultations. In the meantime, I can propose two candidates for two departments. For the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Professor Buha. For the Minister of Internal Affairs, Mico Stanisic. I trust you know the future ministers well enough so that is no need for lengthy explanations here. These two officers have greatly contributed to the affirmation of the Serbian national interests in these difficult times." [Interpretation] Does that mean that you'd already worked with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know him at all. I said that keeping in mind the opinion of people from the party who nominated him. I didn't know him personally. I knew Buha but I didn't know him. So I simply considered that it was the interest of the party, that the party was putting him forward for this post, so I proposed him. I mean, I couldn't really choose. That was the party candidate. And I remember that at that meeting the post of the Defence Minister, I said, would be something that I would be carrying out until further notice, work on preparations of laws and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, just before we recessed, Judge Hanoteau was asking you about comments you made at the 13th session concerning the Minister of Internal Affairs, Mico Stanisic, and we had previously discussed the plans for actions that would be taken in the near future. The Court has already heard considerable evidence about the role of the MUP in the period of time that immediately followed the 12th, 13th and 14th sessions, so I'm not going to direct my attention to Mr. Stanisic or the splitting of the MUP but I wanted to focus for a moment and then move on, on your specialty which you indicated was economics. And in that connection I wanted to turn to the 14th session of the assembly, page 17 of the English, page 19 of the B/C/S. The 14th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly was held on March 27th. And at page 16 and 17 of the English, Mr. Djeric, and page 18 and 19 of the B/C/S, you speak, and if I could turn your attention to page 19 of your version, the fourth paragraph from the top, which begins, "Accordingly we must divide," do you see that? And there you indicate, Mr. Djeric, accordingly we must divide the income and clear up the accounts, the sooner we do it the better. In conformity with our agreement at our last session, I have taken it upon myself to have certain preparations made and I must say that the preparations have been undertaken with the utmost care. The public has been informed that today you adopted a decision on establishing this service affecting the transfer of payments and so forth. I want to you know, however, that as of 1 April, the payment of revenue into the central treasury will cease. Now, that, Mr. Djeric, reflected your efforts and the efforts of the Bosnian Serb authorities toward the economic disempowerment of the Bosnian government, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, as part of the Bosnian government, talks on the regionalisation and decentralisation of power were conducted, so in accordance with that, no accord could be reached because the central powers were in favour of centralism, a unitary state, a centralist state, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you but I'm not asking you why you did it. I'm simply asking you to confirm that this reflected efforts toward the economic disempowerment of the Bosnian government. It's clear enough, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not paying in dues became a practice. These -- this is something that the local units did. They stopped paying in their dues a long time before, and to us it was important to establish order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, that's to say the least disingenuous and you know it. Let's look at your words. I want you to know as of 1 April the payment of revenue into the central treasury will cease. You just told us it stopped before. That's right. It's right there in black and white.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response was sincere. I took an oath for that. The municipalities stopped paying in their funds a long time before. What we are talking about here is that as of April 1st, the service, the public accounting service, was supposed to start operating in the Serbian areas, but as for that whole matter, some municipalities stopped paying their dues in a long time before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was all part of the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into separate ethnic units and the assertion of control and power by the Bosnian Serbs in the areas they claimed, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you because there was no question of the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a question of the restructuring or reorganising of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nobody was in favour of a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they were in favour of finding a solution somewhere between decentralisation and centralisation using the best European experiences in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There would be a separate police, there would be a separate banking structure, but there would be no division? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't necessarily have to mean that. Why would that mean a division, if certain regions were getting organised? Is division to you, for example, the organisation of some European region? Perhaps it would have a constitution or some other things but it doesn't constitute a division. Simply, it was an attempt to reorganise the state. A compromise was being sought. We did have a kind of political maxim and that was the confederation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the maximum, but it would also imply a kind of minimum that everybody would agree on so there was no question of division, the Serbian side never was for the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There are my statements after all. You will never find in any of my statements that Bosnia and Herzegovina was being brought into question. Perhaps I talked about a confederation and also respect for the equality of the peoples, their equality before the law. It's not true to say that there was any talk about division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a couple of other things that you said, then. Yesterday, at page 75 of the transcript, you were asked about a letter of 7 August 1992, that was I think P1248.1 and you were shown that. At this point I'd like to show you P583 tab 119. And again, Mr. Djeric, I'll indicate to you that this is a document that was obtained from the Republika Srpska government archives. As we can tell from the markings, Mr. Djeric, this is a different draft of the August 7th letter. You recognise the signature and stamp that appears on that letter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not complete. I cannot -- this is not complete so on the basis of this I really cannot say anything. You can only see half here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can see the beginning of the letter, I can see the number that is affixed to it 06-25/92, and I can see the end of the letter which says, Dr. Branko Djeric, has a signature and a stamp. What's missing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply do not recall signing documents like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A public statement on behalf of the government was something that would have been drafted by the public information service. I wouldn't do anything like that. Simply I think that this is not quite -- something is not quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the public discovery and the international outcry that followed the discovery of the Omarska camp and the Trnopolje camp was a matter that generated considerable concern among Bosnian Serb officials, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember -- I mean, that there were comments about that. Now, as for concern, well, I think that word would be too strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because these were reception centres, so I do not see any reason for concern in that sense. But at any rate, this created a necessity for us to have this checked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Anything in this document, Mr. Djeric, with which you now disagree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'd have to read it. In principle, I think -- I don't know what the point is for me to agree with a document, I mean, as I've said, I don't remember this and I didn't do that, and I mean, had I done this it would have been different, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not your signature, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that your signature, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature? Well, simply, I mean, well, the document is not mine. I mean, I didn't do this. In the signature, no, I don't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, are you looking at the document bearing the ERN 01246820?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at document 069522.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please look at P583, tab 119, which is 01246820?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take care, perhaps you put it on the ELMO. Second page 01246820 and 21, lower portion, the second page. There we are. A little bit up, Mr. Usher, please. No, to move down the camera or move up the document. That's the same. Yes. A little bit further, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Same question, Mr. Djeric. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I mean, quite simply to put it simply, I mean, I would not sign -- I mean, you see that this was corrected up there, document was corrected. Things were crossed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, why not try to answer? You say, "I'm not sure." Does this resemble -- we have seen -- or at least we have seen a lot of signatures that are supposed to be yours. Does this resemble your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, this is different because in the last part it's not as usual. I mean that is one thing. And well, I mean, I've already answered that. I've given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not sure. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not sign documents like this. Like this. I did not sign documents like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that before. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at tab 21, a letter of May 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 21 of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I think they haven't been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, they have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, tab 21 contains P583, tab 52, a letter to the Honourable James Baker, Secretary of State, Department of State. And it ends with the words, "respectfully yours, Professor Branko Djeric, Prime Minister."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Remember this letter, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24th of May? I mean, well, specifically I don't remember this letter. I remember that there was some correspondence but, say, that specifically I wrote to Mr. Baker, well, no, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you accept or dispute that this is your letter to Mr. Baker?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This letter assures Mr. Baker -- first of all, it begins by noting the most disturbing news coming out of the ministerial conference of NATO suggesting the use of force against the Serbian population and then it goes on to issue a series of denials about what is taking place in Bosnia and emphasises that the Serbian side is holding no hostages, operating no camps, not killing unarmed civilians, and reports, alleging such crimes appearing in the US press and elsewhere are not based on facts. It then goes on to cite population figures, Serb title to arable land reflecting the fact that before World War II genocide was committed against the Serbs by Muslims and Croats and talking about the concentration of Muslims in a few towns of Central Bosnia. Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Djeric, that in the face of possible international reaction to concern about what was being reported from Bosnia, that you on behalf of the Bosnian Serb authorities issued this denial letter to Mr. Baker?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about this --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I don't remember this, because, I mean, well, I'm not the one -- I mean, the foreign minister could perhaps write something like this or -- well, I don't remember. Quite simply, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You remember receiving the disturbing news that there was a possible use of force by the international community threatened in the face of allegations about what Bosnian Serbs were doing to Muslims and Croats in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either, because as for that part of the policy, it was conducted by the Presidency. Policy did not belong to the government. The government did not deal in such matters. This was the exclusive right of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you remember the allegations, the press reports, alleging such crimes appearing in the US press and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember because quite simply I did not have time for that kind of thing. You know, I was preoccupied with social problems. People were homeless. There were enormous problems, vital problems. Problems dealing with life itself. That is what I primarily dealt with. Not this. I didn't have time for this. So for the most part, this was the purview of the work of the Presidency. Karadzic dealt with that, you see? He did for the most part. Koljevic. Up to a degree, Plavsic too. So it was for them, and of course the people around them. I'm primarily referring to the part of the people who were, from a journalistic point of view, like Ostojic. I mean I was well outside that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me get this straight, about 10 days before this letter, you were according to you, at your wits' end because hundreds of Muslim civilians were Bratunac had been taken to Pale and mistreated, right? You told us about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I said, well, I said that there was inhumane behaviour towards them. I said that. And that's what I know. So everything I know I said. And I said everything that I did for these people -- well, to resolve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you told us everything you did? Those people were removed from Pale, and taken outside the territory of RS, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These people from Pale -- well, they were offered -- I mean, well, they were asked and they, well, expressed a wish to be transported to Sarajevo and.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To whom did they express that wish? Did they tell you directly or did you hear it from somebody?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, they heard it from someone else, not from me. I wasn't there at all. I mean, I wasn't in contact with these people. I was just told. Well, I took upon myself to have that problem resolved. And I heard that people wanted to go to Sarajevo and I did everything, as I said, for this problem to be resolved, for these people to be taken to Sarajevo. What else could I have done? I could not have returned them. I mean, it was clear that what was done there was done. I mean, it just could have been, well, worse in a way, simply I was thinking what would be the best for the security and safety of these people at that point in time, for that problem to be resolved temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you learn had happened to these people such that they couldn't go back to Bratunac, they couldn't go back to their homes? You said, "I mean, it was clear what was done there was done."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I don't know about that. I told you about it today. I mean, I told you today with full responsibility that I was not abreast of that at all. This man who mentioned me does not know me at all and he had no previous contact with me. I don't know him at all. So, I mean, I got involved only when I heard that these people were. There somebody brought those people there and just left them there and now on the basis of what, on the basis of what channels, what lines, and so on and so forth, and what kind of service, I don't know, I mean, I cannot tell you anything about that. Except that I got involved in order to have the problem solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You got those people removed via those Muslims, 400 Muslim civilians from Bratunac removed through the exchange commission?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I don't know. Was it the exchange commission? I mean who was there -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You signed the document creating the exchange commission, didn't you, Mr. Djeric? You knew very well what the exchange commission was because you signed that document on May 8th.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, what I signed, I don't know. I don't know. And I don't know whether this commission was involved in this particular case. That is the very beginning. I mean, of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Djeric, the exchange commission went to work right away. Why don't you take a look at tab 1? That's P61, Your Honour. And if you look at page 3 of the English, I believe that conforms to your version as well in B/C/S, you'll see before the list of the 400 prisoners from Bratunac that the document is signed on May 14th 1992 by the member of the government's commission on behalf of the Serbian MUP for the exchange of prisoners of war, Slobodan Markovic. That's how those prisoners were removed from Pale and out of RS territory, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Quite simply, I was not abreast of that. I mean further on. I mean I don't know. I don't know what commission and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djeric, you just finished telling us not too long ago about how you rose to the occasion, outraged, at your wits' end at the presence of these people who had been removed from Bratunac and mistreated and then did everything you could to get them out of Pale so just at what point did you drop the ball and not have any more contact and/or any more understanding of how they were removed from Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, I thought -- I mean, well, that in that way, my role came to an end. I mean, really, I was angry because I was caught unawares. Imagine somebody doing something like that without your knowledge, you don't know anything about it. And you have to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the exchange commission was the vehicle set up for doing precisely that, correct? The official channels went into play and those people were removed. That's what happened, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, this commission belonged to the Ministry of the Interior. I, well, I assume, well, simply, as far as, I mean, well, this was done all over the place, you see, all over the place. I mean, this is a civil war, and there was a conflict, and, well, you know, now, how to protect the population, the civilian population, from all sorts of local people who had some of their own nearest and dearest killed? Well, so that happened. I mean, people were exchanged. But I was not involved in that. Or did I know much about that. It was these ministries that dealt with this, the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of the Interior and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You know very well who else. Let's take a look at the decision to form a central commission signed on 8 May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be what tab, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's included it's tab -- well, it's an extra tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger we have to stop at 7.00 sharp; you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm aware, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the decision, that's P436 and it's the decision on 8 May to form a Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War arrested persons and the bodies of those killed. It lists the representatives, the membership, the representative of the Ministry of Justice, representative of the Ministry of Interior, Mr. Markovic whose name we've seen and a representative of the National Defence ministry and it indicates at the end that the decision will come into effect on the day of its adoption. It is signed and stamped with your name. Mr. Djeric, is that your signature and did you sign that document on 8 May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, well, there is no denying that this commission existed. I just don't know who established it. I mean, I see, well, you know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, Mr. Djeric, would you please answer the question? The question was whether it's your signature and whether you signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, quite simply, I have been caught unawares by these documents. I mean, I do not want, well, you know, I mean, I see that these signatures differ so that keeps me sort of, well, I don't know. I mean -- the signature is a bit different from my signature otherwise. It's a bit different. There are some similarities. At first it is similar and then the other part is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is that you can't confirm that this is your signature. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no more questions. I wouldn't want to run the risk of overrunning the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we adjourn, could I ask the parties whether there is any agreement on the date by which any objections raised to documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. The agreed-upon date would be the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That leaves some uncertainty about admission into evidence of some documents. Is any of the parties intending to then later complain about not being in a position to prepare for final argument for this reason? Apart from the -- well we heard some general complaints on times and I just want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was interested. I notice, Your Honour, added those words at the end to cover the fact that there is a general complaint. It's for the general complaint is a sense of overwhelming in that I doubt whether this particular matter is going to cause us any extra difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one suggestion if we could defer this question to tomorrow to the beginning of the session I want to raise another point with Mr. Stewart, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm entirely agreeable to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask Mr. Usher could you escort Mr. Djeric out of the courtroom but not until after I've instructed him that you should not speak Mr. Djeric about your testimony with anyone, the testimony already given or still to be given. We would like to see you back, quarter past 2.00 tomorrow, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, looking at the number of tabs you have presented, I can imagine that you still would have a lot of questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, the tabs do not in any way represent the number of documents I intend to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could the Chamber conclude that -- could the Chamber take it that you've used your time as you wished and that tomorrow we'll give an opportunity to the Defence to put further questions to Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I hope not, Your Honour. I would ask for some time tomorrow and try to pare it down as much as possible. I've tried to do so. I don't have a great deal more but I think there are some things that are -- would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, in view of what you said earlier, if we would grant 15 minutes to Mr. Tieger tomorrow would that bring you any specific problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where we intend to -- could you please indicate to Mr. Tieger perhaps when you speak to him or to indicate tomorrow morning in court but perhaps discuss this with Mr. Tieger what time you would be able to agree upon without getting into trouble yourself, taking into account that we have to stop at 6.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's helpful, Your Honour. I will certainly do that. May I just say that obviously it would be helpful to have an indication of which of these tabs are not going to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be really valuable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what they call quid pro quo. Could we then hear from the parties tomorrow morning and we'll decide on the basis of what we receive. Perhaps it's good that we have the information not just when we enter the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would be latish tomorrow morning because we are going to see Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Quarter past 2 -- Mr. Josse, could I just add, is the Court intending to have a housekeeping session tomorrow and, if so, how long is that likely to last so that my learned friends can put that into their equation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the Court intends to spend as little time as possible and only the time completely necessary on housekeeping matters tomorrow but perhaps if you have any wishes on housekeeping matters for tomorrow, please convey them to the legal staff of the Chamber and then we'll give you a response prior to the beginning of the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until quarter past 2.00 tomorrow, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
